items.title: Desk clients keep the current goal: one cache, two clients
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
DESK CLIENTS KEEP THE CURRENT GOAL; THE DESK DRIVES VERIFICATION

One cache, two clients
- A desk search answers what the List's rows show: each item's facts.
- A Desk client keeps them: filled once by a search, kept by the desk's published rows, never asked again; after a gap it catches up from its change cursor.
- deskClient takes the rows from the desk's changes answer, which carries, beside its records, the current facts of the items they touched and the held item's panels when one of them is it.
- deskClient fetches on its own, while its agent waits: the current goal's rows, then the one item its agent holds, whole (box, newest chat, checks, files); the agent's reads of it are answered from what it keeps, and only writes go to the desk.
- The Desk app keeps the same: the current goal's rows, and the item open in its dialog, whole.
- One shared block for both: shell/js/spiritData.js with one desk translator, in node and in the page. Bounded: the current goal and the held or open item, newest chat only; older stays a search.
- Desk stays usable all the way; this is a step towards Desk as a face app.

The desk drives verification
- Each item holds its own need for verification, and the desk knows every item's state.

items.title: about the desk-database
items.creator: andy
items.box:
The point of all of it: narrowing the scope of work, traffic, wire and context to the current goal.

- there is a need for two numberic MAIN key fields for desk goals and items.
- the first key must be the goal-number
- the second key must be the item number (always zero for a goal)
- this will easily bound searches within a goal (current goal only mode of searches)
- the cute little ID string you display ('goal/G45.765') can be rendered from those two keys
- searches within the current goal won't catch garbage from other goals anymore.
- No sub-goals and no goal tree: an item never becomes a goal, so two numbers always suffice; the sub-goal mechanism is removed.
- Design mode on goal level AND on item level, so further items can be designed while other items of the same goal already go through their implementation phases.
- A new item always arrives in design mode.
- Tables keyed by goal number and item number: goals and items, chat, and files; each file row holds its grant status.
- The other tables carry the two keys too (the log of writes, the lines, the rules, the docs), so every read is bounded by goal and item; a row about no goal carries goal 0.
- Each side table has its own probability search, filtered by goal or by item.
- The box is a side table of its own, keyed by goal, item and version: each version a row, so the box can grow larger. A client never culls or modifies the data set it mirrors.
- If a bound is needed, the data set bounds itself: a maximum size (about 132 MB) past which it culls its own oldest entries. That is a SpiritOS-wide feature of the data set, managed by no app and no server. The size is one constant, set in a single place.
- Mirror distribution is push: the desk pushes each changed sub-element of a goal or item (a row of a side table) separately, each under PAYLOAD_MAX, so a desk client never grabs anything. A row larger than the payload travels in numbered pieces.
- Reach: when a goal becomes current, the desk pushes it whole onto every desk client; from then on it pushes only that goal's updates. An agent's held item lies in the current goal, so it needs no push of its own.
- A cap is then just one revised box version: the agent writes it, and the desk pushes it like any other change.

chat.text: while you're just waiting you could give me your thoughts on this item.

My thoughts: yes, and it goes deeper than the keys.

- Today the desk has no table of items at all. It keeps only the log of every write (about 92,000 rows now) and rebuilds every goal and item in memory by replaying the whole log, on every search; the desk does that full walk in 38 places.
- The current-goal filter then matches by the goal's member list in memory, and an id is only a string, minted by scanning every item for the highest number.
- Your two numbers would become the key of a real items table, kept up to date on each write beside the log: a current-goal search then reads one goal's rows by its key and never touches another goal, and goal/G33.4 is drawn from the numbers.

Points that need settling in the design:

- The special goals have no number: the plugin goals (Stacks), and the group chat. Your goal/G0 idea from the plugins could cover them.
- Sub-goals: an item can become a goal of its own, so its items would need a third number, or sub-goals get goal numbers of their own.
- A new table is a new persist shape, which by our rules needs a team review before it is built.
- The log stays the record; the table is rebuilt from it if lost.

Which search showed you items from other goals, so the red can reproduce it?
No sub-goals. i don't want a goal-tree. what i do want is: design mode on goal-level AND on item level, so additional items can be designed while other items already go through implementation phases.
so new items will always arrive in design mode

In the box (v2): no sub-goals, so two numbers always suffice and the sub-goal mechanism goes; design mode on the goal and on each item, so new items are designed while others are already being built.

Still open: which search showed you items from other goals?
do we already have well-designed file-tables, chat-tables, all keyed to goals and items ?

No. The desk database has five tables, and none is keyed to goals and items:

- records: the log of every write, numbered in order. An item's chat lines, its files, its checks and its box live only inside these rows, as text, and are rebuilt in memory by replaying the log.
- lines: the older agent and inbox lines, keyed by a string and filtered by date and kind.
- docs: named JSON documents.
- rules and rule_drafts: the desk rules.

So a goals-and-items table, a chat table and a files table, each keyed by goal number and item number, would all be new, filled from the log once and then kept by each write.
where the file tables also hold the a grant-status for the file?
it would make a lot of sense for those other tables to carry the two main key in them, again, about boundaries....

Yes, that fits better than today.

- Today a grant is one G check on the item, covering the whole set of core files in its words; adding one file reopens it for the whole set.
- With a grant status per file row, the commit check asks one row per file it is handed, and a newly added file needs a grant for itself alone.

In the box (v4).

Agreed, in the box (v5): the log of writes, the lines, the rules and the docs carry the two keys as well; a row about no goal carries goal 0.

- The biggest gain is the log: with the keys on every write, one goal is rebuilt from its own rows alone, never by replaying all 92,000.
- Rules and docs that hold for the whole desk sit under goal 0.
these clear goal/iten boundaries for all related data will make the design sooo much cleaner and effective... each of those side tables needs a probability search filtered by goal or item.

In the box (v6): each side table has its own probability search, filtered by goal or by item.

This fits the existing search component: the ranking the desk already uses (goal/G18.5) gets one bounded set of rows instead of everything, so no new ranking is written.
one of those side tables should definitely be the box itself. this would increase its capacity and the client side can drop older versions from it's cache...

In the box (v7): the box becomes a side table keyed by goal, item and version.

- Today every box version is a whole copy inside the log of writes, and replaying the log carries all of them.
- As its own table, one row per version: the newest is read by its key, older versions stay searchable, and a client caches only the newest.
the box table being culled client side can be dropped.

I read that two ways:

- the line about a client culling older versions goes from the box, since a client keeps only the newest anyway;
- or older box versions are dropped from the table itself, keeping only the newest.

Which one do you mean?
it would violate the rule that the client modifies the dataSet
Right: the client culling goes, and the box (v8) says a client never culls or modifies the data set it mirrors.
if anything we'll make the dataSet bounded by a max size and it culls itself, like 132 MB or something....
that would be a SpiritOS glabal feature, not managed by any app or server

In the box (v9): if a bound is needed, the data set bounds itself, about 132 MB, culling its own oldest entries; the app using it never does. That matches how the node database already sheds past its cap.
exactly
In the box (v10): the bound is a SpiritOS-wide feature of the data set, managed by no app and no server.
and 132MB becomes a constant we can modify in one single spot

nudges from the desk to deskClients will essentially be: "changes in "goal-item-tableID" and the desk client can pick up what it needs....

this needs refinement, 

thoughts?

Thoughts, in the order I would refine it:

- A nudge names goal, item, table and the row's new version. A client that already holds that version, its own write for example, does nothing; one that does not mirror that goal ignores it by the goal number alone.
- One write can touch several tables (a claim touches the item, its chat and its files), so one nudge lists every goal, item and table it touched.
- A client keeps one cursor, the newest change it has seen. After a gap it asks once for what changed since then, bounded to the goals it mirrors, and the nudges carry on from there.
- The one tension: our data-flow rule says a mirror is fed by the stream and never asks again. A key-only nudge means one ask per change. A small row (an item's facts, a chat line) could travel in the nudge itself, as the desk publishes rows today, and only a large one (a box) as a key.

Should a small changed row travel in the nudge itself, and only a large one as a key?

the isse here is MAX_PAYLOAD. we need to have a mirror-distribution that transfers sub-elements of goals/items separately... it could be push, which would eliminate all need for a deskClient to go "grab" things....
the desk client only sends it's updates, once a new goal is pushed onto it....

Agreed, and in the box (v12): push, each changed sub-element separately and under PAYLOAD_MAX, so nothing is grabbed.

- One row can still outgrow the payload (a long box). The face already sends a too-large request in numbered pieces and joins them on arrival (G33.1); the push can use the same pieces.
- Push needs to know who mirrors what. The plainest: everyone gets the current goal, and an agent also gets the one item it holds.

Is that the right reach for the push: the current goal to all, plus a held item to its holder?

My reading, now in the box (v13): when a goal becomes current, the desk pushes it whole onto every desk client, and from then on only its updates. A held item lies in the current goal, so it needs no push of its own.

If I read that wrong, say so and I correct the box.
yes, the work (pushing etc...) will still center around the "current" goal as a scope
this is all about narrowing scope of work/traffic/wire/context etc....
so when i say cap al the agent does, is push a revised box back.

A measurement for this item, from my deskClient's own log of its asks to your desk over the last two hours:

- Every desk ask takes 3 to 6 seconds on average, even the smallest: a box release 2.6 s, a chat line 6.4 s, the longest 12.5 s, past what my side waits. That is where my timeouts and your duplicate lines come from, not from the new cache.
- The cause matches this item: each of those asks replays the whole log of writes, 93,000 rows now.
- 63,000 of those rows, two thirds, are agent.state: an agent saying listening or working each time it waits. They are kept forever and replayed on every ask.

So the keyed tables would cure the wait, and agent.state needs no row in the log at all; it is a live state, not a record.
